    AI Overview
    April Fools' Day, celebrated on April 1, has uncertain origins, but is widely linked to the 1582 calendar shift in France
    . When France adopted the Gregorian calendar, moving New Year's from late March/April 1 to January 1, those slow to adapt were mocked as "April fools". Other theories include ancient Roman festivals like Hilaria. 
    • The 1582 Calendar Switch (France): King Charles IX adopted the Gregorian calendar, changing the New Year from April 1 to January 1. People who forgot or were slow to learn of the change continued celebrating in late March/April 1 and were mocked, receiving fake gifts or being sent on "fool's errands".
    • Ancient Festivals (Hilaria): Some historians trace it to the ancient Roman festival of Hilaria (late March), where people dressed in disguises and mocked one another.
    • Spring Equinox Theory: Many cultures have traditionally celebrated the start of spring and the renewal of life around this time, often involving lighthearted trickery to mark the uncertainty of the season's weather.
    • Poisson d'Avril (April Fish): In France, a common tradition is to tape a paper fish to someone's back, a practice dating back centuries. 
    While popular in Europe from the 16th century onward, the exact historical moment the tradition began is still debated by historians.

    On April 1 every year, millions of people relish in the opportunity to pull harmless pranks and practical jokes. Though April Fools’ Day is widely celebrated throughout the English-speaking world, historians haven’t yet pinned down a definitive date or time for its emergence. Though it’s clear the holiday has existed in some form since at least 1500s, competing theories attribute the holiday to medieval England or more modern France. Others insist the holiday is rooted in even older celebrations of spring in ancient Rome and elsewhere. Despite its murky origins, some textual evidence suggests the holiday could be over 600 years old. Folklorist Stephen Winick lays out three compelling contenders: one from England, two from France. The custom of playing pranks on April 1 could date back to the Middle Ages—and evidence of its emergence may have been documented by English poet Geoffrey Chaucer.
